title: Tu B'Av
hook: the fifteenth of Av, once a day when young women danced in white in the vineyards (Mishnah Taanit 4:8)

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Valentine: a martyr whose story is mostly lost, and a day for saying it on paper. Your line was a note. Who got yours? Today, a much older day of love, and the end of the week. Day eight hundred seventy-five.

Rows of vines outside Jerusalem. Young women walk out between them, all dressed in white, and begin to dance. It sounds like the opening of a romance, but it's in the Mishnah, a collection of Jewish law and teaching, at the close of a section about fast days. In the middle of all that seriousness, a rabbi stops to remember a day of pure joy. Its name is a date on the Hebrew calendar: the fifteenth of the month of Av. Today: Tu B'Av.
screen: `ROWS OF VINES.` → `ALL DRESSED IN WHITE.` → `A RABBI REMEMBERS JOY.`

segments.voice: First, the saying. In the Mishnah, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says, in plain words, that Israel had no days of joy like the fifteenth of Av and the Day of Atonement. On those days, the daughters of Jerusalem went out in white garments, and danced in the vineyards. Second, the detail that makes the passage. The white garments were borrowed, the Mishnah says, so as not to shame anyone who had none of her own. Rich or poor, nobody could tell. On a day about love, the first act was a kindness about dignity. Third, what they said. The young women called out to the young men, in plain words: lift up your eyes and see whom you choose; don't look at beauty, look at family. The Mishnah then reads a line from the Song of Songs about a king on the day of his wedding, and the gladness of his heart. Fourth, the name. Tu is the number fifteen written in Hebrew letters, and Av is the month. So the name of the holiday is simply the date. The vineyard dances belong to the past. Some Jews mark the day today as a day for love, for weddings and for matchmaking, and it is a happy turn in a month that also holds the mourning of Tisha B'Av. This week we've traced love's edges: boundaries, loving yourself, small acts, listening, grief, and a note. Tu B'Av adds one more: when love dances, nobody gets left out of the white.
screen: `NO DAYS OF JOY LIKE THESE.` · `THE WHITE BORROWED.` · `LIFT UP YOUR EYES.` · `THE NAME IS THE DATE.` · then, large: `TU B'AV.`

segments.voice: Let the breath slow. Bring to mind a time someone made sure you weren't left out: an invitation, a seat saved, a coat lent, a word that put you on equal footing. Stay with that memory for a breath or two. Now bring to mind one person around you who might be on the outside right now. Someone new, someone quiet, someone who doesn't have the right thing to wear, in whatever sense. Let one small way to include them come to mind. If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Tu B'Av. The fifteenth of Av, a day the Mishnah remembers for borrowed white dresses and dancing in the vineyards. Today's word.

Your line: dance in white. Wear something white today if you like, and let it remind you of the borrowed dresses: make one small move so someone near you isn't left out. Day eight hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Some Jews today mark Tu B'Av as a day of love, with weddings, matchmaking events and celebrations, and Jews who study the Mishnah read about it in tractate Taanit.

what it means: the fifteenth of Av, which the Mishnah remembers as a day of joy, with dancing in white in the vineyards.

notes: Mishnah Taanit 4:8 is paraphrased throughout (no public-domain translation on the list); a Judaism Keeper should confirm: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's saying, the borrowed white garments, the young women's words (the Mishnah's wording includes 'don't set your eyes on beauty, set your eyes on family'), and the closing citation of Song of Songs 3:11.
'A hillside near Jerusalem' is scene-setting; the Mishnah says the daughters of Jerusalem went out to dance in the vineyards.
'At the close of a section about fast days' places 4:8 at the end of tractate Taanit; confirm.
Modern observance ('some Jews mark it today', and its contrast with Tisha B'Av earlier in the month) should be checked.
